txt: Not a muscle moves in her face, but her eyes trace yours, stern and perceptive.
She doesn't say anything.
She looks as if pondering whether to answer or not... but then shakes her head slightly.
She says nothing; her glare speaks for her.
She shrugs. Almost no reaction.
She sounds almost helpful: "What you *can* do right now is go back to your station and write a *report*."
The cold look in her eyes speaks louder than words: she is not amused.
The woman turns to you, calmly: "As you can see, these men can only take so much baseless scrutiny. I'm doing my best to keep the situation civil, but..." What follows is a slow headshake.
"*Even* a mod..." Her face stiffens. "Glen, I went to *law school*. I am an attorney."
"*This* is what I studied law for?"
"Aaaand here we go. Back to the usual." The woman sighs.
"Aggressive? You make your living enforcing violence. These people are just *dock workers*."
"Anodic dance music, you wouldn't get it."
"Are you deaf? There will be no singling anyone out. You can't arrest *a* Hardie boy without arresting *all* Hardie boys."
"Babysitting imbeciles... what the heck, Liz?"
"Before? After? *During?*" She shakes her head slowly. "I seriously advise you to stop testing these men. They're getting *agitated*."
"Before? After? *During?*" She spreads her arms. "This is getting ridiculous. They told you what happened. Stop wasting your time."
"Can't wait to change out of these rags."
"Detective Disorientated." She smiles coldly. "Are you still wondering where you are? This is Martinaise, in case you've forgotten. I advise you not to overstay your welcome."
"Detective Skin-Colour." She smiles coldly. "I'm still black as you can see. Do you have any more keen-eyed observations?"
"Disregard the outburst, officer." She gives Titus a condescending glance. "None of the boys have any more comments on their power relations. That night they acted as one. That's all."
"Do you think you could do that? Do you think you could arrest them all?" A shadow of a smirk passes her lips, as she tilts her head.
"Evrart *personally* sent me to take care of this. If this goes south we'll all be in the shit -- but you, Titus Hardie, are going to be buried. Am I understood?"
"Evrart isn't paying me enough for this."
"Fine. I'll tell him. After a long walk along the *coast*." She walks off without looking back.
"Fine." She hands you her pair of yellow gardening gloves.
"For the record..." she steps in, forcefully. "Titus Hardie did not explicitly specify the *victim* as a whore. Nor did he say anything about trusting her."
"Get sober." Her expression stiffens. "Do your *job*. Ask your questions and get the hell out of Martinaise."
"Glen..."
"He said no such thing." She accidentally raises her voice. "This isn't about me."
"Hjelmdallermen."
"I am a *legal counsel*," she intones. "Don't make this personal."
"I am not," she says dryly.
"I don't need privatization paeans from a rent-a-cop." Her expression stiffens. "Just do your *job*. Ask your questions. Then get out of Martinaise."
"I guess it's fair to say you guys have it on life support."
"I have heard about your *medical condition*. People talk. And I have no patience for it. Or pity."
"I represent the Union and these men here." She points to the crew around the table. "Don't make this personal."
"I suggest not wasting time on trivial pleasantries and focusing on why you are actually here -- Titus Hardie," she points to the tall man by the table.
"I will." It doesn't look like you changed her mind.
"I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union. I've been watching you." It feels like she's waiting for a reaction of some sort.

"I'm being aggressive?" She raises her eyebrows. "Listen, you Moralintern lackey, you're part of a mob, enforcing the unlawful privatization of Revachol. Twenty fat men in the Occident are stealing it all -- and you are their body guard."
"I've got nothing to say to you. Why are you wasting your time?" She crosses her arms.
"I. Don't. Care."
"If anything, it is the RCM who *do* things to people..." She shakes her head. "But we digress."
"If there's any *post-mortem* trauma, it's your problem. This will not turn into a cross-examination."
"It's beyond the horizon for you."
"Let him go, Titus." The woman raises a hand, as if to draw the giant's attention away from you. "I'm sure he doesn't need it."
"Let me handle this," the woman says to the crowd in the mess hall before turning to you...
"Let's." Her expression stiffens.
"Let's."
"Like I already told you, I'm a legal counsellor." She crosses her arms. "Do you have hearing problems?"
"Listen, please!" She raises both hands. "This cop and this drumhead court martial won't decide who..."
"Listen, you Moralintern lackeys. You're a mob, enforcing the unlawful privatization of Revachol. Twenty fat men in the Occident are stealing it all -- and you're their body guards."
"Look -- a comedian." Her expression stiffens. "Do your *job*. Ask your questions. Then get out of Martinaise."
"Look, we're not discussing your taste in music anymore, officer. Do you have questions for my clients or not?"
"Maybe wrap it up instead?" She doesn't even look at you.
"My answer is no."
"No one is emotional here." Her expression stiffens further. "Do your *job*. Ask your questions -- then leave."
"No one is going to kill anyone. Let's just put the guns down and talk like civilized human beings."
"No, Glen -- they aren't." Her tone is cold and uninvolved.
"No, I'm not a gardener, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms.
"No, you don't. What you have is seven honest men, who thought it forthcoming to tell you what happened -- so that you don't waste any more of your time."
"No," she steadies her breathing. "Not disco. Disco is *undead*."
"No. Talk to Titus."
"No. You did not get an answer. Titus does *administrative* work. He pushes paper. Fills out forms -- the others can't read. But on that night they all acted as *one* man."
"No." It doesn't look like she's into popular adventure-fantasy.
"No." The woman interjects. "These *seven* honest men have *equally* come forth. They told you what happened -- so that you don't waste any more of your time."
"No."
"Nothing," her reply comes sharp. "Your investigation here is done. Leave Martinaise, go back to your stations, where you belong."
"Nothing," her reply comes sharp. "Your investigation here is done. You should go back to Jamrock -- to your station, where you belong."
"Obviously I'm a lawyer. A legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms. "I would urge you to consider what you say to my clients."
"Of course, and I'm just an epidermochromatic counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union," she says without blinking an eye.
"Of course, you were just doing your *job*... I'm not a gardener, by the way, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms.
"Officer Discotheque." She smiles coldly. "Still wondering if we listen to disco? We don't, by the way. We don't listen to disco anymore."
"Okay, enough. All of this is irrelevant to your stated investigation."
"Okay, you have a dictionary. That doesn't mean you get it..."
"Over here!" She snaps her fingers.
"Please do."
"Please try to control yourself in the presence of *visitors*, Titus." Her voice is a bit softer than earlier.
"SHUT UP, ANGUS!"
"So ask what you came to ask -- or get back to your commanders."
"So let's get to it -- you're looking for Titus Hardie. You think he has information that will help you. Maybe he does." She points to the man on her right.
"Stop it. This is a waste of everyone's time." She sounds agitated. "I think we have already established that you're not going to single anyone out."
"Sure, reacting to stimuli... I'm not a gardener, by the way, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms.
"Sure, you were *curious*... I'm not a gardener, by the way, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms.
"TITUS HARDIE!" Her voice rings through the room like a warning shot.
"That's Titus. Talk to him. But know this: I'll be keeping an eye on you. No strong-arming, nothing official. The district of Martinaise does not recognize your authority to make arrests."
"That's enough insinuation for today, Titus." She turns to you. "Officer, your interview is drawing to an end. Don't waste your last questions."
"That's for the courts in Le Jardin to decide, not for the officer making an arrest. Which we all know you won't be."
"That's more like it, boys." She turns to you. "You heard him, it was Angus on all fours. Anything else you need to know?"
"That's right, I'm not a gardener, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." It feels like she's waiting for a reaction of some sort.
"That's right, I'm not a gardener, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms.
"The Union isn't going to *do* anything to you. It is not a crime syndicate, it is a labour organization."
"There is no catch. These seven honest men have all *equally* come forth to tell you what happened -- so that you don't waste any more of your time."
"This is a misunderstanding. Nothing irreversible has happened yet. You can just return to your unit and forget all about this."
"This is about your alcoholism, isn't it? People talk." She squints. "I have no patience for it. Or pity."
"This line of questioning is *over*," the woman interrupts. "You got the cause of death already. Hanging."

"This line of questioning is *over*," the woman steps in before you can answer. "You got the cause of death already. Hanging. If there's any *post-mortem* trauma, it's your problem. This will not turn into a cross-examination."
"Titus has already given you a cause of death. Hanging. Why is it so hard for you to understand?" The question is rhetorical.
"Titus is hiding nothing." She turns to the hulk of a man. "Titus..."
"Titus, I'm amazed. Where is the same professionalism when it comes to *other* topics? You're doing great. I hardly have to interfere at all."
"Titus, do *not* answer. You have been forthcoming enough."
"Titus, you don't have to clarify anything."
"Titus, you were told to keep a low profile."
"Titus..." He looks at her.
"Unbelievable..."
"Vulgar idiot," she shakes her head.
"What are we going to *do* to you?" She starts laughing. It's a cold laughter, devoid of joy.
"What you want is of no significance, *officer*. Don't test your authority -- in Martinaise you are no one."
"When Titus Hardie says he *runs* the Hardie boys," the woman adds, "he means that in an *administrative* capacity. On that night everyone acted as *one* man."
"Why are you so fucking FAT, Angus?!" Lizzie snaps at him. "Now it's all pointless, because of *you*. You wasted my time. I told you, Titus --" she turns to him. "I told you to just give her up."
"Why don't you go home and log it into evidence. These men have told you what happened."
"Yes, extremely normal... I'm not a gardener, by the way, I'm a legal counsellor for the Dockworkers' Union." She crosses her arms.
"Yes, there are *some* administrative differences," she gives Titus a stern look, "but on that night they all acted as *one* man."
"You are looking for Titus Hardie, who you think has information on a murder the RCM is investigating. You want to interview him." She points to the man standing in the middle of the room.
"You don't have to answer any of his questions," the fixer turns to remind Titus.
"You might want to start asking your questions now. It's not going to get better than this."
"You should."
"You're all drunk, come to your senses!" She sounds very sure of herself. "You won't gun down seven people in the middle of the street. This isn't a frontier town or a jungle outpost."
"You're far from home, *lieutenants*... This isn't a district known for its love of self-proclaimed militiamen."
"You're far from home, *officer*... This isn't a district known for its love of self-proclaimed militiamen."
"You're not here to chat up the legal counsel, you're here to question these men."
"You're right. I shouldn't have."
